2027-06-07.title: Monday of the Tenth Week in Ordinary Time
readings: the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction
Taste and see the goodness of the Lord
Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven
2027-06-07.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 10 (Year I). This week the first reading begins the Second Letter of Paul to the Corinthians, and the Gospel begins the Sermon on the Mount, which will be read on the weekdays of the next two weeks. The psalm is given in NRSV numbering (Lectionary Psalm 34:2–9 = NRSV 34:1–8). Liturgical colour: green.
2027-06-07.verse: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.
theo: The Second Letter to the Corinthians is the most personal of all Paul's letters. He wrote it around the year 55 or 56, probably from Macedonia, after a painful time with the church he had founded in Corinth: a visit that went badly, a letter written “with many tears,” rumours that he was unreliable, rivals who mocked his weak appearance. We will read it for the next two weeks, and we will meet a Paul who is tired, wounded and yet full of hope. He does not begin with a defence. He begins with a blessing: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our affliction.” The Greek word for consolation, paraklesis, rings through these few verses again and again. It is the word from which the Holy Spirit gets his name, the Paraclete, the one called to stand beside us. Paul does not say that God keeps him out of trouble. He says that God meets him inside it, and that the comfort he receives is not meant to stop with him: “so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction with the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God.” Suffering and comfort both flow outward. “For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ.” The Christian who has been comforted becomes a channel of comfort. The Psalm sings the same experience in the voice of a poor man rescued: “This poor soul cried, and was heard by the Lord, and was saved from every trouble.” And it ends with an invitation: “O taste and see that the Lord is good.”

In the Gospel Jesus sees the crowds, goes up the mountain and sits down, as a teacher sat in his day, and his disciples come close. Matthew wants us to remember Moses, who went up Sinai and brought down the Law. Here a greater than Moses gives the law of the kingdom, and he begins not with a command but with a blessing, eight times over. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.” The Beatitudes turn the world's idea of happiness upside down. The world calls happy the rich, the strong, the people who never cry and never lose. Jesus calls happy the poor in spirit, who know they need God; the meek; those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; the merciful; the pure in heart; the peacemakers; those persecuted for righteousness' sake. The Beatitudes are first of all a portrait of Jesus himself, the poor, meek, merciful, pure and persecuted Son. They are also a promise. “Those who mourn” are not told to stop crying; they are told “they will be comforted.” Paul and Matthew meet in the same word. The God of all consolation is the one who fulfils the Beatitude. In Kerala this is the week when schools reopen after the summer and the monsoon rain has arrived: new books, new uniforms, wet umbrellas at the gate. The Church opens her own school today, the Sermon on the Mount, and its first lesson is that happiness is a gift of God given to the humble.
outline: Ask: when you were sad or in trouble, who comforted you, and how?
Point 1 · The God of all consolation
Paul begins a hard letter with a blessing, because God meets us inside our affliction.
Point 2 · Comforted in order to comfort
The consolation we receive is meant to flow on to others.
The Beatitudes: Jesus calls blessed the poor, the mourners, the meek and the merciful.
“Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.”
live: Think of one comfort God gave you in a hard time, and today offer the same kindness to someone going through something similar.
Choose one Beatitude, write it on a slip of paper, and ask Jesus to grow it in you this week.
2027-06-07.prayer: Blessed are you, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Father of mercies and God of all consolation. You have comforted us in our troubles more times than we can count. Make us channels of your comfort to all who are afflicted: the sick, the grieving, the lonely, the poor. Lord Jesus, you taught on the mountain that the poor in spirit, the meek and the merciful are blessed; give us hearts like yours, emptied of pride and open to your kingdom. Bless the children and teachers beginning a new school year, and keep them safe in the rains. Amen.
altar: At every Mass, before Holy Communion, the priest prays that we may be kept “safe from all distress” as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Saviour. Then he lifts the Host and says: “Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb.” The Beatitudes of the mountain end at the altar. Here the poor in spirit are fed, the mourners are comforted, and the pure in heart receive the One they long to see.

quick: Paul begins his most personal letter by blessing the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who comforts us in every affliction.
The comfort we receive from God is meant to flow on to others who suffer.
Jesus opens the Sermon on the Mount with the Beatitudes: the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek and the merciful are blessed.
2027-06-07.action: Visit, call or message one person who is suffering today, and bring them a little of the comfort God has given you.
2027-06-07.question: Which Beatitude do I most need to grow into, and which do I most resist?

family.explain: Jesus went up a mountain and sat down to teach. He told his friends who are the really happy people in God's eyes: not the people who have the most toys or money, but people who are humble, kind, gentle, who make peace and who have clean hearts. St Paul says God comforts us when we are sad, so that we can comfort others.
family.intention: We pray for children and teachers starting the new school year, and for families who are sad or in trouble.
family.ask: Ask: “Which of Jesus' blessings can each of us live at school or at work this week?”

illus: On the first day of school in a town in Kottayam, a boy in the third standard stood crying at the gate because his father had died during the vacation and he did not want to go in. An older girl, who had lost her own mother two years before, left her friends, took his hand and said: I know; I cried too; come, sit with me today. She walked him to his class and came back at the lunch break. Their teacher said later that the girl had done what no adult could have done, because she knew from the inside what he felt. She had been comforted, and she passed the comfort on. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Father of mercies, God of all consolation, comfort us in our troubles and make us comforters of others. Teach us the happiness of the Beatitudes. Amen.
share: God consoles us in all our affliction so that we may console others (2 Corinthians 1:4). When did God comfort me, and whom could I comfort with that same comfort?
Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted (Matthew 5:4). Is there a grief in my life that I have not yet brought to Jesus?
Blessed are the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3). What does it mean for me to be poor in spirit at home or at work?
pm.resp: Taste and see the goodness of the Lord.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a place of comfort for all who are afflicted.
For those who mourn the death of someone they love, that they may be comforted.
For children, students and teachers beginning a new school year, and for safety during the monsoon rains.
For Christians persecuted for righteousness' sake, that they may know the reward Jesus promised.
For our group, that we may comfort one another as God comforts us.
pm.close: Lord Jesus, you are the meek and humble of heart. Make our hearts like yours, and lead us to the kingdom promised to the poor in spirit. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today we begin to read St Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians. Paul had been through a very difficult time with this church. People were saying bad things about him; he had been hurt, and he had hurt them with a strong letter. You might expect him to begin with complaints. Instead he begins with praise: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation (2 Corinthians 1:3).

Notice what Paul does not say. He does not say that God took away all his problems. He says that God consoles us in all our affliction. God does not always take us out of the storm; he comes and sits with us in the boat. And Paul says why: so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction (2 Corinthians 1:4). The comfort God gives us is not a private treasure. It is meant to be passed on.

Think of the people who comforted you best when you were in pain. Very often they were people who had suffered something similar. A mother who had lost a child, a man who had lost his job, a friend who had been sick. Their own wounds, healed by God, made them gentle with yours. That is what Paul means. Our sufferings, united with the sufferings of Christ, can become a source of comfort for others.

In the Gospel Jesus begins the Sermon on the Mount with a list of surprising blessings. Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted (Matthew 5:4). The world does not call these people happy. Jesus does, because God is close to them. This week, as children go back to school, let us go back to the school of Jesus. Let us be humble, merciful, peacemaking. And let us pass on the comfort we have received. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever fallen down and hurt your knee? Who came running to help you? Maybe your mother, or a friend. St Paul says God is the God of all comfort: he comforts us when we are sad, so that we can comfort others. And Jesus told his friends on a mountain who the truly happy people are: people who are kind, gentle, who make peace and who have clean hearts. This week at school, look for a child who is sad or alone, and be a comforter for Jesus!

intro: A God who comforts us in affliction, a comfort that flows on to others, and the upside-down happiness of the Beatitudes.

sub: Paul begins with blessing, not complaint.
God meets us inside our affliction.
q: Comfort, O comfort my people, says your God.
For just as the sufferings of Christ are abundant for us, so also our consolation is abundant through Christ.
points.apply: Tonight, recall one hard moment in your life when God comforted you, and thank him for it by name.

sub: Comfort is not a private treasure.
The Church as a community of consolation.
q: The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit.
Our hope for you is unshaken; for we know that as you share in our sufferings, so also you share in our consolation.
points.apply: This week visit or call one person who is going through a trial you have known yourself.

sub: Blessed are the poor in spirit.
q: O taste and see that the Lord is good; happy are those who take refuge in him.
Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
points.apply: Choose one Beatitude for this week and ask the Lord each morning to help you live it.

concl: Paul blesses the God of all consolation, who comforts us in every trouble so that we can comfort others.
Jesus calls blessed the poor, the mourners and the meek, because God's kingdom and God's comfort belong to them.
2027-06-07.resolve: Each day this week, pass on to one person the comfort God has given you.
